title: Account takeover through identity proofing and recovery flows

threat_model.actor: Anyone able to reach the login, registration, recovery, or step-up surface, including a caller holding a valid credential or reset token for an account they legitimately own
threat_model.asset: Control of an account and the identity assertions downstream systems derive from it
threat_model.trust_boundary: The proof the caller presented and the account the flow ultimately acts on
threat_model.failure_mode: A recovery, enrolment, or step-up path binds the operation to a subject taken from the request rather than from the proof, or applies its second factor on some paths and not on the one that completes the change
threat_model.impact: An account is taken over without its credential, or a second factor that is enrolled and believed effective is never actually required on the completing request

required_evidence: The application authenticates users and can change or restore a credential without an existing session
A recovery, verification, or step-up artefact is issued to one subject and later redeemed on a separate request

signals: A reset or recovery handler accepts both a token and an account identifier in the same request body
The account is loaded by email, username, or phone number after the token has already been validated
Completing a credential change does not revoke sessions, refresh tokens, or API keys issued before it
Step-up or re-authentication is applied from a list of paths kept separately from the route registrations
The dispatcher falls through to a handler when a path is absent from the enforcement list
A route has been renamed or versioned while the enforcement list still names the previous path
A factor can be enrolled, replaced, or disabled using only the primary credential
The verified state of a challenge is read from a client-supplied field rather than from server-side state
Backup codes, trusted devices, or remember-me records survive a credential reset
A reset service validates a token fingerprint and then resolves the account from the posted address
A recovery router enforces step-up from a path set that no longer matches the registered route

boundary.subject: the account the presented proof was issued for
boundary.object: the account whose credential, factor, or contact address the request changes
boundary.invariant: The account a recovery or step-up operation mutates is the account named by the proof, and every path that completes the mutation requires the same proof

examples: Phone number update used for one-time codes
Session minted at the end of a recovery flow
Long-lived refresh token issued after step-up
Reset request response that differs for known addresses
Timing difference between known and unknown accounts

signals: Trace the subject from the presented proof to the write, and record every point where a request field could substitute for it
Enumerate every route that can complete a credential or factor change, including versioned, mobile, and administrative variants, and compare their guards
Find where the enforcement decision lives relative to the route registration, since a separate path list drifts when routes are renamed
State the intended proof for each transition of the account lifecycle and compare it with the guard the code actually applies
Decide whether an unknown route, an unresolved identity, or a failed lookup fails closed or falls through to the handler
Check whether a credential change is defined to invalidate prior sessions, refresh tokens, and device trust, and whether the code performs it
Establish the lifetime, single-use property, and storage form of reset and challenge artefacts, and whether the record stores the subject
Look for long-lived artefacts that survive a credential change: remember-me cookies, API keys, backup codes, trusted devices
Use two synthetic accounts, request a proof for the first, and attempt to complete the flow against the second
Exercise the owned-account control first, so a later denial is distinguishable from a broken harness
Replay the completing request against every sibling route to see whether any of them omits the step-up requirement

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and create two isolated synthetic accounts that hold no real personal data
Complete the flow normally against the owned account first and record the exact request and response
Repeat the completing request with the proof for one account and the identifier of the other, and record which account changed
Enumerate sibling and legacy routes for the same operation and record which of them enforce the second factor
Record the artefact lifetime, whether it is consumed, and whether prior sessions still authenticate after the change

false_positive_filters: The account is loaded from the proof record and the request identifier is only compared against it, never used to select the subject
A gateway, middleware, or framework guard enforces step-up before the handler, evidenced in configuration rather than assumed from the architecture
The suspected route is unregistered, disabled by a flag, or unreachable from any caller-controlled entrypoint
The artefact is single-use and bound to the subject in storage, so a token for one account cannot select another
The observed difference between known and unknown accounts is required by the documented product behaviour and is accepted with a stated rationale

required_evidence: The proof the caller must hold, and the field the code actually uses to select the account
A reachable path from an unauthenticated or lower-privileged entrypoint to the credential or factor write
A safe reproduction with two synthetic accounts that shows which account was mutated
The defective invariant stated as a binding or coverage failure, and the concrete impact on account control
refutation_tests: Re-read the handler for a comparison between the proof's subject and the request identifier before concluding the binding is missing
Look for the guard in middleware, a gateway, or the framework's route configuration rather than only in the handler body
Repeat the flow against the caller's own account to distinguish a general failure from an authorization decision
Check whether the artefact is already single-use and subject-bound in storage, which would make the request identifier inert

root_causes: The subject is taken from the request body while the proof carries its own subject, so the two can disagree
Step-up enforcement is keyed by a path list that is maintained separately from the routes it is meant to cover
An unknown or unlisted route falls through to its handler instead of failing closed
A credential change does not invalidate the sessions, tokens, and device trust issued before it
One flow in the account lifecycle is protected while a sibling flow that reaches the same sink is not

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Derive the subject only from the proof, verify the request identifier against it rather than instead of it, and require the same proof on every route that completes the change
patterns: Store the subject on the artefact and load the account from that record, treating any request identifier as a value to compare
Declare the step-up requirement as part of each route's registration so a rename cannot silently drop it
Fail closed for unknown routes rather than dispatching to a handler
Consume the artefact before the write and bound its lifetime, so a replay cannot reach the sink twice
Revoke sessions, refresh tokens, API keys, and device trust as part of the credential change transaction

assertions: The vulnerable reset variant applies a credential change to the account named in the request rather than the one on the token record
The remediated reset variant loads the account from the token record, rejects a mismatched identifier, and revokes prior sessions
The vulnerable recovery router completes the flow with no second factor because the enforcement list names a path that is no longer registered
The compensated recovery router enforces step-up for a handler that contains no second-factor logic of its own, and fails closed on unknown routes
Both remediated variants still complete the legitimate flow, so the assertion distinguishes enforcement from an unconditional refusal

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: Rate limiting, bot defence, and delivery-channel controls frequently live outside the repository and change what an enumeration difference is worth
The synthetic fixtures prove the contract shape, not behaviour on an external identity provider or a hosted authentication service
Where identity is delegated to an external provider, the binding under review may be the provider's, and the code cannot answer it alone
Absence of a guard in a handler is not absence of enforcement until the middleware and gateway configuration has been read
